title: Ukraine's Largest Drone Maker: Nearly 100,000 a Month, AI Interception Is Just the First Step
dek: Ukrainian drone maker General Cherry produces nearly 100,000 drones a month, with interceptor drones costing about $2,000 to shoot down Russian Shaheds worth over $50,000. AI guidance is battle-tested, but full autonomy remains distant.
why: This episode offers a rare, direct account from a top Ukrainian drone maker of the real shape, costs, and limits of AI on the battlefield. Dense with information, it's directly valuable for understanding modern warfare and the drone industry.
who: Founders, investors, and engineers focused on modern warfare, the drone industry, and military AI applications.

points.h: Producing nearly 100,000 a month, and still scaling
points.body: Founded in 2023, General Cherry initially made only about 10 drones a month; now it produces around 100,000 (the exact figure is confidential). The company works with more than 110 military brigades, and the best units burn through over 5,000 drones a month. Production is still expanding because the battlefield consumes drones at a ferocious rate — they have become expendable.

points.h: Hundreds of drone companies, but only 10–15 at the top
points.body: Ukraine may have as many as 2,000 drone companies, but most are garage-sized operations. Only 10 to 15 large firms can produce 1,000 to 10,000 drones a month, and General Cherry says it ranks in the top five. This fragmented, sprawling ecosystem is the basis of Ukraine's rapid innovation, but it also means fierce competition.

points.h: AI models built in-house, co-developed with the military
points.body: General Cherry's AI guidance system is entirely self-developed, backed by a strong R&D department, and built in close cooperation with different frontline units. They get daily feedback from mobile teams on the ground and iterate quickly. This R&D-to-combat-to-feedback loop lets Ukrainian drone tech adapt to the battlefield fast, rather than relying on outside procurement.

points.h: The rocket-shaped FPV came from Red Bull, not Ukraine
points.body: The rocket-shaped FPV drone is not a Ukrainian original — Red Bull first used it for sports events in 2021 or 2022. Ukrainian companies found the shape could reach higher speeds than a standard quadcopter, so they adopted and optimized it. It reflects the industry's fast-learning pragmatism: not originality, but what works.

General Cherry's interceptor drones (such as the Bullet) cost about $2,000, yet can shoot down Russian Shahed drones that cost $50,000 to $100,000. This asymmetric cost exchange is key to Ukraine's response to Russia's saturation attacks — using cheap drones to exhaust expensive enemy assets while avoiding wasting Western-supplied air-defense missiles.

points.h: Confirmed kills of over 5,000 Russian drones
points.body: General Cherry's tactical interceptor drone (General Trajectory Air) has confirmed more than 5,000 kills of Russian drones since production began in February 2025; in December alone it shot down over 1,000 Russian Moniya drones. The Shahed-interceptor model entered mass production in December 2025, with confirmed kills approaching 1,000. These numbers show interceptors have become a significant force in battlefield air defense.

points.h: AI runs on the device, not in the cloud
points.body: General Cherry's AI guidance model runs on the drone's onboard camera chip, not in the cloud. The operator detects the target by radar, launches the drone, and the AI automatically identifies and locks on — no human intervention needed. This on-device AI avoids battlefield communication delays and jamming, which is why it works in practice.

points.h: Fully autonomous weapons are a terrifying future, but AI is inevitable
points.body: Marko admits that if drones become fully autonomous, it will be terrifying — killing would no longer require another person, just a robot or drone. For now they use semi-autonomous AI only on interceptors, because adding AI to ordinary FPVs would raise costs significantly, and it's better to buy more non-AI drones. But he predicts AI will spread quickly and prices will fall, making future battlefields even more brutal.
